claim: When adding a Loop Cut (Ctrl+R) whose curvature should match a nearby existing edge, don't leave it partway between two reference edges by eye -- press E to make the cut 'even' (snap its shape to match one specific existing edge exactly) and press F repeatedly to flip which of the two flanking edges (indicated by a highlighted red dot) it conforms to, landing the new loop precisely on the desired edge's contour instead of an imprecise in-between shape.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 0:35-1:50 (screen-key overlay on): 'when you use this Loop cut... you can see that it's choosing the shape of the edge which is closest to it as you drag it over... what you can actually do is if you hit E, it will actually now copy the shape of your choosing regardless of where it is between that... the Red Dot which is showing you which Edge it's taking the form on is now out at the top, so if I hit F again you can see that I'm changing that.'
rejected_alternative: Dragging the loop cut to an eyeballed position between the two reference edges, leaving its curvature ambiguous
reason: A loop cut positioned only approximately by eye won't cleanly match either neighboring edge's shape, leaving a visible kink; snapping it exactly to one edge's shape via E/F removes that ambiguity.

claim: For redirecting the flow of an edge loop around a shape (so faces route around a corner instead of splitting into a T-junction), the video explicitly rejects the Rotate Edge operator (Ctrl+E) in favor of manually deleting the face between two target vertices and merging them together (Alt+M, choosing 'At Last' to snap to a known-good vertex position).
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 8:17-8:56: 'there's one operation where I think you take this, you hit control E and then you can rotate the edge, but I don't like doing it because it's really hard to orient... it's hard to sort of see things, I like to just see what's actually going on instead of tweak things myself, so this is how I would do it: first of all I would delete this face... and then Alt+M, at last, and now you can see that this line is correct.'
rejected_alternative: Ctrl+E Rotate Edge to reflow the edge loop
reason: Rotate Edge changes the mesh in one unpredictable jump that's hard to visually orient and control; explicitly deleting the face and merging chosen vertices to a chosen target lets the modeler see and control exactly where the geometry ends up.

claim: To force an edge loop to flow around a corner instead of splitting into an unwanted branch (a T-junction), identify the two vertices that should become a single point, delete the face between them, select both vertices, and merge with Alt+M choosing 'At Center' -- this creates the single joining vertex needed to redirect the face flow. Afterward, slide any remaining loose vertices together with a double-tap G, then clear leftover geometry with Remove Doubles (W) and Delete > Edge (X, choosing Edge, not Vertex, so the now-redundant connecting edge is removed without deleting the merged vertex).
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 3:28-5:41: 'the way you merge things, merging two vertices in blender, is you hit Alt M... a little popup will ask you where do you want the merged piece to be, you can choose the first vertex, the last vertex, or in our case I want one in between so I'm just going to choose At Center'; then, after selecting remaining vertices, 'double tap G and slide this across... W, remove doubles... hit X and then make sure you delete the edge not the vertex.'
reason: Manually choosing the merge target (At Center vs At Last vs At First) controls exactly where the resulting point lands, which determines whether the surrounding face flow reads as one clean edge or leaves a visible kink.

claim: When deleting an unwanted Loop Cut that only exists to support a curve the mesh no longer needs (because reference photos show the surface actually goes flat at that point), selecting the loop's vertices and choosing Delete also removes the vertical edges that pass through those same vertices, producing broken geometry. Instead, switch to Edge select mode, Alt-click to select only the horizontal edges of the unwanted loop, then choose Delete > Edge Loops -- this removes just the intended loop and leaves the vertical structure intact.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 12:09-12:42: 'if you did this you would see this horrible mess, and the reason for that is that you're also deleting these lines that are going vertically, so instead switch to Edge select and then just select the horizontal lines holding down alt as I click on them, now I select delete and then Edge loops and now it is correctly deleted them.'
rejected_alternative: Selecting the loop cut's vertices directly and using Delete, which also deletes the connected vertical edges
reason: Vertex-based deletion can't distinguish 'the horizontal loop I want gone' from 'the vertical edges passing through the same vertices that I want to keep'; edge-mode selection plus Delete > Edge Loops targets only the intended loop.

claim: When a fully-encircling Loop Cut would correctly sharpen a wanted corner but also unacceptably sharpen an unrelated edge elsewhere on the same continuous loop (here, the anvil's horn, which must stay smooth), and there is no easy way to reroute the loop around just the wanted corner without creating a triangle or ngon, the modeler's judgment call is to add the loop cut on only one side of the corner rather than both -- producing a corner that reads noticeably sharper than doing nothing, but less crisp than a fully two-sided corner -- treating this as an acceptable, explicitly-weighed tradeoff rather than a problem to solve completely.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 17:52-19:18: 'what about a loop cut here, problem is solved, however just like what we were trying to avoid doing, that adds a loop cut all the way along our model... there's not really an easy way to add one in this direction, however if you were to add one in this direction... it's not as sharp as if you were to have one here as well, generally you want to have them on both sides but... it really becomes a question of like how much value do you put on this problem... honestly I think it is enough.'
rejected_alternative: Adding the loop cut on both sides of the corner for full sharpness (rejected because it would also sharpen the horn edge), or spending significant extra time rerouting the topology to avoid the tradeoff entirely
reason: Perfect sharpness on every edge isn't free -- it can force unwanted sharpness elsewhere on the same topological loop; deciding how much time a given imperfection is worth fixing is treated as an explicit, named tradeoff rather than left as an unexamined shortcut.

claim: Before committing to a fully sharp edge (via added supporting geometry or a Crease), check reference photos for how sharp that edge actually is on the real object -- the video's actual final choice was to skip the geometric loop-cut solution just discussed and use only a Crease (Shift+E) on the indent's corner, specifically because reviewing reference photos showed the edge is 'pretty smooth on like every reference photo,' so a fully hardened edge would have been less accurate than the softer crease-only approach.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 19:22-20:01: 'the method actually that I used for my final model was even lazier than this, I didn't even have that, all I did was I just made this a crease, I hit Shift E and pulled that out... but looking at reference photos I actually realized like that's pretty smooth on like every reference photo I saw, it's fairly smooth there, so we don't actually want that completely sharpened edge, it has to catch some light.'
rejected_alternative: Fully hardening the edge with a loop-cut-supported sharp edge, assumed correct by modeling instinct without re-checking the reference
reason: An edge that instinctively 'should' be sharp can be measurably softer on the real reference object; checking before committing avoids over-sharpening a surface the source material actually shows as smooth.

claim: Default solid-shading view can hide subtle unwanted creases in a mesh. Switching the viewport shading dropdown to a Matcap (Display icon > matcap selection) changes the surface's lighting response and can reveal faint creases or shading errors that weren't apparent under the default material/lighting -- useful whenever visible shading artifacts depend on how light happens to be hitting the surface at the current camera angle.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 20:09-20:47: 'not sure if you can see it... here's a little tip, if you go to display, no shading, and click on matcap, there's a number of different types of shading you can use here, this is especially helpful when you're sculpting something and the light just isn't hitting it just right... so you can see with this one I'm now able to see that we've got what looks like a crease here and a crease here.'
rejected_alternative: Relying only on the default solid-shading lighting to spot creases, which can miss artifacts depending on the current light angle
reason: Crease visibility under solid shading depends on the current lighting angle; a matcap with a different, more revealing light response surfaces problems the default shading was hiding entirely.

claim: How much time to invest perfecting a given edge loop's flow should scale with whether the mesh will ever deform -- for a static hard-surface prop (this anvil) that will never be animated, small topology imperfections are an acceptable tradeoff for time saved, whereas the same imperfection on a mesh that WILL deform (the video's example: a character's eyelid meant for a hero in a movie) would be worth spending hours getting exactly right, because deformation exposes topology flaws that a static render does not.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 21:37-22:23: 'some people would look at this and say oh that's horrible what you've done, but really, unless you were animating this... if this was the eyelid of a character that was going to be a hero in a movie, you would spend hours making sure that every single edge loop was perfect, but you've only got a finite amount of time to make anything and for something like this you've got to weigh up all the choices... this solution, as ghetto as it looks, is actually working pretty fine.'
rejected_alternative: Treating every topology imperfection as equally worth fixing regardless of whether the asset will ever deform
reason: Investing perfect-topology effort uniformly regardless of end use wastes time on static assets where the imperfection will never be exposed by deformation, while under-investing on assets that will deform (rigged characters) risks visible artifacts.

claim: Before applying a Mirror modifier (a destructive, effectively-irreversible operation after which edits to one side no longer mirror to the other), duplicate the object first and move the duplicate to a separate 'trash' collection/layer purely as a backup, so the pre-apply version can be recovered if a mistake is discovered later.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration at 22:35-23:00: 'first we need to actually just apply the mirror... first of all, just before you apply anything, make sure that you duplicate it and then move it to a trash layer just so that you've got a copy of it in case you need to go back, now I'm going to apply that mirror.'
rejected_alternative: Applying the Mirror modifier directly on the only copy of the object with no backup
reason: Applying a modifier collapses it into the base mesh; keeping a duplicated, unapplied copy in a separate collection is a cheap insurance policy against needing to redo mirrored edits from scratch.
